title: Before Supermarkets, Brown Eggs Were a Sign of Poverty
fullText: For over a century, brown eggs were the cheapest eggs in America. They sat unsold at the back of city markets. Nobody with money wanted them. They were the eggs of poverty, of immigrant families, of subsistence farmers who could not afford better birds. Then sometime in the late 20th century, the price flipped. Brown became premium. And the story of how that happened has almost nothing to do with eggs and almost everything to do with how easily we let marketing decide what food is worth. Walk into any grocery store in America today and head to the egg aisle. The white ones sit on the bottom shelf, plain carton, generic label, a couple of dollars. The brown ones sit higher up, sometimes in a rustic looking cardboard container stamped with words like farm fresh, all natural, cage-free. They cost more, sometimes a dollar more, sometimes two. And if you are like most shoppers, you assume the difference in price reflects a difference in quality. That the brown eggs are the better eggs, the healthier eggs, the eggs that come from happier chickens living on some sundrenched farm with a red barn and a wooden fence. That is exactly what the egg industry wants you to believe. But the real history tells a completely different story. Rural America, 1800s. Before refrigerators, before highways, before the invention of the grocery store as we know it, eggs moved a very short distance from where they were laid to where they were eaten. There was no cold chain, no distribution centers. If you lived on a farm, you had chickens. If you had chickens, you had eggs. And the breed of chicken you kept said something about who you were. In the same way that the condition of your barn or the quality of your plow said something about you. Early American poultry production was by modern standards barely production at all. The National Chicken Council describes it simply. Many households had backyard flocks of dualpurpose chickens. These chickens supplied eggs and an occasional chicken for Sunday or holiday dinner. That was it. You kept a few birds. They gave you breakfast. And when they got old, they became soup. Wealthy land owners and commercial operations, the ones selling eggs in city markets and supplying restaurants, tended to keep white leg horns. These were sleek, energetic birds originally imported from the Italian port city of Levoro. Brought to North American shores as early as 1828. Captain Gates arrived in Mystic, Connecticut in 1852 with one of the first significant leg horn imports. By the 1870s, the breed had caught on fast. Leggh horns were not much to look at. They were small, nervous, and loud with disproportionately large combs and a restless energy that made them difficult to handle. But they had one quality that made them irresistible to anyone trying to make money from eggs. They were prolific layers. A single leg horn hen could produce up to 300 eggs a year. And because the birds were small, they ate less feed per egg than any other breed. From an economic standpoint, a leg horn was a tiny feathered factory, and leg horns laid white eggs. Meanwhile, the farmers who could not afford to specialize, the subsistence families, the immigrants from Eastern Europe, and the British Isles who brought their own poultry traditions with them, the rural households scraping by with a few birds in the yard. They kept different breeds. Rhode Island Reds, Plymouth Rocks, Orpingtons. These were bigger, sturdier chickens. What the industry calls dualpurpose breeds. They laid eggs, yes, but not as many. And when they stopped laying, they became dinner. They were practical birds for people who could not afford to keep an animal that only did one thing. And every single one of those breeds laid brown eggs. So in the markets of Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, a pattern emerged. White eggs arrived in bulk from the commercial leg horn operations outside the city. Packed neatly in wooden crates, sorted by size, uniform in color. Brown eggs showed up in smaller quantities carried in by farm wives and hired hands, often in simple baskets, varying in shade from pale tan to deep reddish brown. The color of the shell became an unspoken code. White meant professional, scale, someone who knew what they were doing. Brown meant small, poor, someone who probably also grew turnips and mended their own fences. The upper classes in America's growing cities began to see brown eggs the way they saw a lot of things that came from the rural margins. Rough, unsophisticated peasant food. If you ran a fine restaurant in Manhattan in the late 1800s, you ordered white eggs. If your household staff was shopping for a wealthy family on the Upper East Side, they reached for white without being told. Hotels specified white eggs in their kitchen orders. Bakeries that served high-end clientele used white eggs because the pale shells looked cleaner in the minds of their customers, even though the shells never ended up in the pastry. Brown eggs, meanwhile, were what you ate if you did not have a choice. They sat at the edges of farmers markets. They were sold for less. And in the minds of urban consumers who were rapidly losing any connection to how their food was actually produced, the brown shell became a mark of inferiority that had nothing to do with the egg itself. Nobody stopped to ask whether the color of a shell had anything to do with what was inside it. If you cracked a brown egg and a white egg into the same bowl, you could not tell them apart. The yolks were the same, the whites were the same, the nutrition was the same, the taste was the same, [music] but that did not matter because the judgment was never about the egg. It was about the person who produced it. You just knew white was better, brown was not. And this quiet, unspoken prejudice was a warning sign because it was not really about eggs at all. It was about a larger system taking shape. A machine that would soon swallow the American food supply whole and reshape what people ate, how they ate it, and what they believed about it. A handful of smallcale poultry farmers in rural counties could see what was coming. They watched the commercial operations grow larger. They watched the prices drop lower. They watched their brown eggs get pushed further and further toward the edge of the market stall. But nobody was going to listen to them because that machine was about to find its perfect bird. By the early 1900s, the white leg horn was no longer just a popular chicken. It was becoming the only chicken that mattered. The commercial egg industry, still young but growing fast, had figured out the math. A leg horn ate less, laid more, and produced a uniform white egg that city buyers already preferred. Every other breed was a compromise. The leg horn was pure efficiency. Then came the cages. In the 1920s, poultry researchers began experimenting with a system borrowed from an unlikely source. For centuries, ships had kept chickens in small wooden coups hung like canary cages to supply eggs during ocean voyages. The principle was simple. Confine the bird, collect the egg, minimize waste. In the 1930s, commercial farms adapted this idea into what would later be called the battery cage. Rows and columns of small wire enclosures stacked inside warehouses, each one holding a single hen. The results were staggering. One worker could now manage 500 birds. The hens never touched their own waste, which reduced disease. Feed could be measured and distributed with mechanical precision. and the eggs rolled gently down a sloped wire floor onto a collection belt, clean and uniform, ready for market. After World War II, the system exploded. Labor shortages pushed farms toward anything that could reduce the number of hands needed. Feed science had advanced enough that nutritionists could formulate a complete diet in a single mash, eliminating the need for hens to forage at all. Vaccines for poultry diseases like Newcastle and foulpox developed in the 1930s and4s meant that birds packed into close quarters no longer died at catastrophic rates. Every technological breakthrough made the cage system more profitable. And every profitable farm that switched to cages put pressure on neighboring farms to do the same or go under. Now, all of this history might sound like background detail, but understanding what happened next requires understanding just how completely the Legghorn won this race. By the early 1960s, conveyor belts had replaced hand collection entirely. Eggs moved from hen to washer to carton without a human finger touching them. The scale was almost incomprehensible compared to what had existed just 40 years earlier. In 1920, a farm with 400 hens was considered large. By 1960, operations housing tens of thousands of birds were becoming standard, and by 1990, an estimated 95% of all laying hens in the United States lived in battery cages. The battery cage was not designed for any specific breed, but in practice, it was built for the leg horn. These birds were small enough to thrive in tight spaces. They were calm enough not to injure themselves against the wire, and they just kept laying day after day, month after month, 300 white eggs per hen per year. The larger heritage breeds, the Rhode Island Reds and Plymouth Rocks that laid brown eggs, were too big, too active, too temperamental for cage life. They needed space. They needed to scratch and forage. They were not built for confinement. So the industry did not ban brown egg breeds. It simply left them behind. At the same time, the American government was building the infrastructure that would make white eggs the national standard. The USDA began developing voluntary egg quality guidelines in the 1920s. As the growth of a national egg market made standardization necessary, what they valued was predictability, clean shells, uniform size, consistent appearance. A white egg met every one of those criteria before it even left the farm. A brown egg, with its natural variation in shade, from light tan to deep chocolate, looked inconsistent by comparison. It looked unregulated. It looked to the eyes of a government grader, like it came from somewhere that did not have its act together. Then the supermarkets arrived and the brown egg lost its last foothold. Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly in Memphis, Tennessee in 1916, and it changed grocery shopping forever. It was the first self-service grocery store in America. Before Piggly Wiggly, you walked up to a counter and told a cler what you wanted. The cler went to the back, retrieved your items, and brought them to you. You never saw the shelves. You never compared products side by side. You trusted the cler or you trusted the brand name. And that was the end of it. After Piggly Wiggly, you walked through aisles and picked products off shelves yourself. Piggly Wiggly was also the first grocery chain to install refrigerated cases, which meant perishable goods like eggs could sit on display for hours under bright lights while customers browsed. By 1922, there were,200 Piggly Wiggly stores in 29 states. The Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company, better known as A and P, was even bigger, operating thousands of locations across the country. These chains needed something that small town general stores never did. They needed visual uniformity. When you are selling eggs by the thousands of dozens across hundreds of stores, you need every carton to look like every other carton. You need the customer in Memphis to open the same looking product as the customer in Chicago. White eggs delivered that they were bright, clean, and identical. Under the fluorescent lights of a new supermarket, a carton of white eggs looked almost clinical in its perfection. A carton of brown eggs with their slightly varying shades looked like something from a different era. And so brown eggs were pushed to the margins. Not by law or regulation, but by pure economics. The farms that raised leg horns could produce eggs cheaper, faster, and more uniformly than anyone raising heritage breeds. Supermarkets bought from those farms because the price was right and the product was consistent. Consumers bought white eggs because that was what supermarkets stocked. And the cycle reinforced itself year after year, decade after decade, until brown eggs all but vanished from the American mainstream. By the middle of the 20th century, around 90% of the eggs sold in American supermarkets came from white leg horns or their commercial descendants. If you walked into a grocery store in Kansas or California or Texas, you might never see a brown egg at all. All except in one stubborn corner of the country. New England never stopped buying brown eggs. The Rhode Island Red had been developed right there in Little Compton, Rhode Island in the early 1800s when Chinese chickens brought to New England aboard Yankee Clipper ships were cross-bred with local stock. The result was a hardy reddish brown bird that became one of America's first recognized domestic breeds. It was woven into the region's identity the way maple syrup or clam chowder was. Generations of New England families had grown up cracking brown eggs into cast iron skillets, and no amount of leg horn efficiency could shake that habit. In the 1970s and 80s, the New England Brown Egg Council ran a television jingle so catchy it became a regional anthem that people still remember decades later. Brown eggs are local eggs and local eggs are fresh. The slogan was clever because it sidestepped the one fact that would have undermined the entire campaign. There is no nutritional difference between a brown egg and a white egg. None. The color of the shell is determined entirely by the breed of the chicken. A brown egg from a factory farm and a white egg from a freerange operation are on the inside the same product. The New England Council knew this. So instead of claiming brown eggs were healthier, which they could not prove, they claimed brown eggs were local, which in New England happened to be true. It was technically honest and it was devastatingly effective. That regional loyalty, that stubborn New England insistence on brown eggs would soon look less like nostalgia and more like prophecy. Because while the rest of the country was drowning in cheap white eggs, something was shifting in the American relationship with food. And brown eggs, the poverty eggs, the peasant eggs, the ones that city shoppers had rejected for over a century, were about to get a second chance that nobody in the egg industry saw coming. Everything the egg industry had built around white was about to work against it. In 1962, a marine biologist named Rachel Carson published a book called Silent Spring. It was an investigation into the effects of synthetic pesticides on wildlife and human health, and it detonated like a bomb across American culture. President Kennedy ordered a federal investigation into her claims. Congress began drafting environmental legislation. And ordinary consumers, for the first time in decades, started asking uncomfortable questions about where their food actually came from and what had been done to it before it reached their plates. Carson did not write about eggs. She did not mention chickens. But Silent Spring cracked open something much larger. It made Americans suspicious of industrial food production in a way they had never been before. And that suspicion would only grow. By the late 1960s and into the 1970s, a full-blown counterculture food movement was taking shape. Health food stores began appearing in college towns and urban neighborhoods, catering to a growing community of consumers who wanted nothing to do with the factories, the chemicals, or the corporate supply chains that had come to dominate American agriculture. J I Roddale, who had been publishing organic farming and gardening magazine since the 1940s to almost no audience, suddenly found himself at the center of a cultural shift. His ideas about composting, natural pest control, and chemical-free growing, once dismissed as eccentric, were now the philosophy of an entire generation. The natural and organic food movement was small and ridiculed in 1962. Within two decades, it would reshape the American grocery store from the ground up. And here is where the brown egg re-enters the story. The counterculture did not just want different food. It wanted food that looked different. Food that signaled a rejection of the industrial system. White bread was out. Whole wheat was in. White rice was suspect. Brown rice was trustworthy. White sugar was poison. Raw honey was medicine. White flour. White milk in plastic jugs, white margarine in white tubs. All of it was coded as artificial, processed, corporate. The color brown across the entire grocery store had become a visual shorthand for natural, wholesome, and real. It was not a scientific distinction. It was an aesthetic one. But in the grocery aisle, aesthetics are everything. Brown eggs fit this new mythology perfectly. They looked like they came from a farm. They looked like something your grandmother might have collected from a backyard coupe in the countryside. They looked, in a word, authentic. And the fact that brown eggs had been associated with small farms and rural poverty for over a century only made the association stronger. The counterculture was not running toward luxury. It was running towards simplicity. And brown eggs looked simple. The egg industry noticed and the egg industry adapted. If you are finding this helpful, consider subscribing. We cover stories like this every week. The hidden history behind the everyday things you never think to question. Now, where were we? Producers who had spent decades breeding leg horns for maximum output began quietly expanding their brown egg operations. Not because the eggs were different on the inside, not because consumer demand had shifted based on any nutritional evidence, but because brown eggs could be sold for more money. According to Phil Lumpert, a grocery industry analyst, brown eggs typically carry a 10 to 20% premium over white eggs at the register, regardless of whether they are labeled organic or free range. That margin applied to a product that Americans consume by the billions adds up to a staggering amount of money extracted from consumers based on nothing more than pigment. Then in 1990, Congress passed the Organic Foods Production Act, which directed the USDA to create national standards for organic products. This was the moment the brown egg found its permanent home on the top shelf. The organic certification process was expensive and producers who invested in it needed a way to visually distinguish their organic eggs from conventional ones. Brown shells became that distinction. Not because the regulations required it, not because organic hens could only be brown egg breeds, but because if you are charging twice the price for a product, it helps if it looks different from the cheaper version sitting right next to it. Brown eggs became the uniform of the organic aisle. and the association between brown shells and better farming became nearly impossible to undo in the consumer's mind. The marketing strategy was elegant in its dishonesty. Supermarkets began placing brown eggs next to the organic and freerange labels. Not because brown eggs had to be organic, not because freerange hens only laid brown eggs, but because the visual association reinforced a story that consumers already wanted to believe. brown shell, green label, words like pasture-raised, and all natural. A carton made of recycled looking cardboard instead of styrofoam. Every element of the packaging was designed to trigger the same feeling. This is the good egg. This is the real egg. This is the egg worth paying more for. And it worked. If you are wondering how that is even legal, so is everyone else. Because there is nothing illegal about charging more for a product that is identical to a cheaper one as long as you do not make a specific false claim. The egg industry never said brown eggs were healthier. They never had to. They just put them in the right packaging on the right shelf next to the right labels and let the consumer's brain do the rest. The New England exception suddenly looked less like a regional quirk and more like a preview of the entire country's future. For decades, New Englanders had been paying more for brown eggs based on regional loyalty and a catchy jingle. Now, the rest of America was doing the same thing, except they were paying the premium based on a feeling that had been carefully manufactured by the very industry they thought they were rejecting. The breeds that made this reversal possible were the same ones that had been poverty markers a century earlier. Rhode Island Reds, Plymouth Rocks, the same sturdy dualpurpose birds that immigrant families and subsistence farmers had kept in their backyards because they could not afford to specialize. Those breeds now commanded higher prices per egg than the leg horn, the bird that had built the entire commercial egg industry. That is the kind of irony that makes economists cry. And the reversal did not stop at branding. Factory farms began raising brown egg breeds in the exact same industrial conditions as their white egg operations. The same battery cages, the same automated feeding systems, the same warehouse scale confinement. A hen producing brown eggs in a modern commercial facility lives an identical life to a hen producing white eggs in the facility next door. The only difference is the color of the shell and the price on the carton. The consumer who reaches for the brown eggs because they want to support a better, more humane system of farming is in most cases buying the same system in a different rapper. The consumer who chose brown would look back on this moment and wish they had asked harder questions. But in the grocery aisle under fluorescent lights with 30 seconds to make a decision, the brown egg just felt right. And feeling, not fact, is what drives most of the choices we make about food. And this is the part where things stopped being funny. Because the brown egg premium is not just a harmless quirk of consumer psychology. It is a case study in how marketing can take a product with no meaningful difference, attach a narrative to it, and extract billions of dollars from people who believe they are making an informed choice. The egg aisle is a mirror and what it reflects back is not flattering. Consumer awareness is growing, but the pricing gap has not closed. Not even close. Here is what the science actually says. Shell color is determined by breed genetics. Period. A hen's earlobes of all things are a reliable predictor. Hens with white earlobes tend to lay white eggs. Hens with red or brown earlobes tend to lay brown eggs. The pigment called protoperin is deposited on the outer surface of the shell during the final hours of egg formation inside the hen. If you scratch the surface of a brown egg, the white shell underneath is revealed. Every egg starts white. The brown is just a coat of paint. The yolk color, which many consumers also associate with quality, is determined by the hen's diet, not the breed. A henfed maragold petals or corn, will produce a deep orange yolk. A henfed wheat will produce a pale yellow one. You can get a rich golden yolk from a white egg and a pale watery yolk from a brown one. The shell tells you nothing about what is inside. Crack a brown egg and a white egg into the same bowl and you cannot tell them apart. A food scientist at the University of California put it simply. Consumers have come to believe that brown eggs are healthier, which they are not. So why do we keep paying more for them? Because the human brain is wired to trust visual shortcuts, especially when it comes to food. White is an industrial color. It suggests sterility, factories, fluorescent lighting. Brown is an earthy color. It suggests soil, barns, hand gathered baskets. These are not rational assessments. They are emotional reflexes. And the food industry has spent decades learning how to trigger them. A 38 country survey by the International Egg Commission found that egg color preferences are almost entirely cultural, shaped not by science, but by whichever breeds of chicken were first domesticated in a given region. The Irish, French, checks, Hungarians, Portuguese, Nigerians, and British overwhelmingly prefer brown eggs. Canadians, Fins, Americans, and Indians prefer white. In the United Kingdom, 99% of eggs sold are brown. In Mexico and Iran, 98% are white. In China, roughly 65% of eggs are brown. While in South Africa, the split runs in the opposite direction. And here is the detail that proves the whole thing is arbitrary. In the United Kingdom, white eggs are now the premium product. They are the rare ones, the special ones, the ones that cost more. The exact opposite of the American market. Same egg, same nutrition, completely different story attached to it depending on which side of the Atlantic Ocean you happen to be standing on. In countries where consumers mostly buy white eggs, they tend to view brown as more nutritious. And in countries where brown is the default, white starts to look exotic and desirable. The less common color always becomes the premium product. It has nothing to do with the egg and everything to do with scarcity and perception. What the egg aisle really reveals is not a difference in eggs. It is a difference in stories. And the story we tell ourselves about food, about what is natural, what is healthy, what is worth paying for, is almost never based on evidence. It is based on association, on packaging, on color, on the vague, unexamined feeling that one thing is better than another because it looks the way we think good food should look. The modern brown egg sits on the top shelf of an American supermarket in a recycled cardboard carton stamped with a pastoral illustration of a red barn and a sunrise priced at 10 to 20% more than the white eggs below it. 150 years ago, that same egg sat at the back of a city market unsold because no one with money wanted it. The egg did not change. The chicken did not change. The nutrition did not change. The only thing that changed was the story. And that might be the most uncomfortable thing about this entire history. Not that the egg industry tricked us, but that we were so willing to be tricked. That the same shell produced by the same family of breeds could mean poverty in one century and premium in the next. And most of us never stopped to notice. If stories like this change the way you see the world around you, that video on screen right now goes deeper into one of the biggest pricing illusions in your kitchen. Click it. I will see you there.
fullTextVi: Trong hơn một thế kỷ, trứng nâu là loại trứng rẻ nhất ở Mỹ. Họ ngồi không bán được ở phía sau chợ thành phố. Không ai có tiền muốn có chúng. Họ là những quả trứng của sự nghèo đói, của những gia đình nhập cư, của những người nông dân tự cung tự cấp có thể không đủ khả năng mua chim tốt hơn. Sau đó vào khoảng cuối thế kỷ 20, giá đã đảo chiều. Màu nâu trở thành cao cấp. Và câu chuyện chuyện đó xảy ra như thế nào hầu như không liên quan gì đến trứng và hầu hết mọi thứ liên quan đến việc chúng ta dễ dàng để bộ phận tiếp thị quyết định loại thực phẩm nào là có giá trị. Ngày nay, hãy bước vào bất kỳ cửa hàng tạp hóa nào ở Mỹ và đi đến lối đi bán trứng. Những cái màu trắng nằm ở kệ dưới cùng, thùng carton trơn, nhãn chung, một cặp của đô la. Những cái màu nâu đặt cao hơn, đôi khi được đựng trong hộp bìa cứng trông mộc mạc có đóng dấu với những từ như trang trại tươi, hoàn toàn tự nhiên, không có lồng. Chúng có giá cao hơn, đôi khi nhiều hơn một đô la, đôi khi là hai đô la. Và nếu bạn giống như hầu hết người mua hàng, bạn cho rằng sự khác biệt về giá phản ánh sự khác biệt về chất lượng. Rằng những quả trứng màu nâu là những quả trứng tốt hơn, những quả trứng khỏe mạnh hơn, những quả trứng đến từ những chú gà hạnh phúc hơn sống trong một trang trại ngập nước nào đó có chuồng đỏ và một hàng rào gỗ. Đó chính xác là điều mà ngành công nghiệp trứng muốn bạn tin tưởng. Nhưng lịch sử thực tế lại kể một câu chuyện hoàn toàn khác. Nông thôn Mỹ, những năm 1800 Trước tủ lạnh, trước đường cao tốc, trước sự phát minh ra cửa hàng tạp hóa như chúng ta biết nó, trứng di chuyển một khoảng cách rất ngắn từ nơi chúng được đẻ đến nơi họ đã bị ăn thịt. Không có dây chuyền lạnh, không có trung tâm phân phối. Nếu bạn sống ở một trang trại, bạn có nuôi gà. Có gà thì có trứng. Và giống gà mà bạn nuôi đã nói lên điều gì đó về con người bạn. Tương tự như tình trạng chuồng trại của bạn hoặc chất lượng của cái cày của bạn đã nói điều gì đó về bạn. Việc sản xuất gia cầm thời kỳ đầu ở Mỹ theo tiêu chuẩn hiện đại hầu như không được sản xuất. Hội đồng Gà Quốc gia mô tả nó một cách đơn giản. Nhiều hộ gia đình có đàn gà lưỡng dụng ở sân sau. Những con gà này cung cấp trứng và thỉnh thoảng một con gà cho bữa tối Chủ nhật hoặc ngày lễ. Đó là nó. Bạn đã nuôi một vài con chim. Họ đã cho bạn bữa sáng. Và khi già đi, chúng trở thành súp. Những chủ đất giàu có và hoạt động thương mại, những người bán trứng ở chợ thành phố và cung cấp cho các nhà hàng, có xu hướng giữ sừng chân trắng. Đây là những con chim có kiểu dáng đẹp, tràn đầy năng lượng ban đầu được nhập khẩu từ thành phố cảng Levoro của Ý. Được đưa đến bờ biển Bắc Mỹ vào đầu năm 1828. Thuyền trưởng Gates đến Mystic, Connecticut vào năm 1852 với một trong những quan trọng đầu tiên sừng chân nhập khẩu. Đến những năm 1870, giống chó này đã phát triển nhanh chóng. Sừng Leggh không có gì nhiều để nhìn. Họ nhỏ bé, lo lắng và ồn ào với những chiếc lược lớn không cân xứng và một nguồn năng lượng không ngừng nghỉ điều đó khiến họ khó xử lý.
